analysis.one_liner: Exempts pistols fitted with stabilizing braces from federal registration and tax requirements.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a hearing or vote before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the federal definitions of 'rifle' and 'shotgun' so that any pistol fitted with a stabilizing brace — an arm support intended for one-handed firing — no longer counts as a short-barreled rifle or shotgun. That would take those firearms out of the National Firearms Act, which requires owners of covered weapons to register them with the government and pay a tax. The bill was introduced by Senator Lankford with six Republican cosponsors and never advanced past the committee stage.
analysis.who_benefits: People who own or want a pistol with a stabilizing brace, including many shooters with disabilities, who would avoid the National Firearms Act's registration process and its $200-per-item tax. Firearms and brace makers would also gain a larger market for brace-equipped pistols.

how_it_helps.text: The bill removes any pistol equipped with an arm brace intended for one-handed firing from the legal definitions of 'rifle' and 'shotgun', taking it out of the National Firearms Act and its registration requirements.

The text explicitly says that documented use of the firearm with two hands or firing from the shoulder cannot be used to prove the owner did not intend one-handed firing, so owners would not lose the exemption based on how they actually shoot.
The change would take effect immediately on enactment.

analysis.who_pays: No one pays a direct cost. The cost is a policy one: many short-barreled firearms would leave the National Firearms Act's registration system, which is how the government keeps records of certain weapons and screens their purchasers.
analysis.who_pays_short: The federal firearms registry and the public

drawbacks.text: The bill's exception turns on the owner's intent to fire one-handed, but the text says documented two-handed or shoulder firing does not disprove that intent [S3]. That makes the carve-out very hard to police, since nearly any brace-equipped pistol would qualify regardless of how it is used.

The National Firearms Act's registration and tax apply to rifles and shotguns with barrels shorter than the legal minimum [S2]. Removing brace-equipped pistols from that system would mean many functionally short-barreled firearms would no longer be registered or go through the process tied to that registration.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For brace owners the benefit is real but modest: avoiding a $200 tax and a registration process that can take months. The cost is that the exception is written so broadly — an intent standard that cannot be disproven — that it effectively exempts a wide class of short-barreled firearms from registration with no way to separate disability aids from de facto short rifles. A narrower draft tying the exemption to genuine disability use would have been easier to defend.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and sat there with no hearing, no vote, and no further action until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Lankford introduced the bill on April 7, 2022; it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day.
Six Senate Republicans cosponsored the bill.
The action history shows no further action — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — after the referral, through the end of the 117th Congress in January 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The status quo held: brace-equipped pistols remained under existing federal firearms rules, and the National Firearms Act's registration system and the regulatory authority over braces were left unchanged. Because the bill was low-stakes and never moved, no one gained or lost much, though the firearms industry kept operating under the pending regulatory uncertainty the bill aimed to clear up.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo: existing firearm rules stayed in place

for.name: Sen. James Lankford
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to exempt brace-equipped pistols from the National Firearms Act.

sides.party_line_note: Only Republicans sponsored and cosponsored the bill, and it never reached a vote, so no record of how the parties would have split exists.

industries.note: The bill would exempt brace-equipped pistols from the National Firearms Act's registration and $200 tax, removing a barrier to buying those products and expanding the manufacturers' customer base. Their gain runs alongside the interest of shooters, including disabled shooters, who use the braces; the cost falls on the public in the form of fewer registered short-barreled firearms.
